open_obligations: Note that LLM judges stand in for humans, so the second half of Leike et al.'s question is not directly tested.
Check whether the debaters are much stronger than the judges on each closed task.
Check whether the mixed result is driven by task-specific factors such as GSM8KQA arithmetic.
in.other_title: Closed QA without information asymmetry: debate vs direct QA depends on judge strength
in.rationale: Leike et al. ask whether debate works beyond fact-checkable statements and whether judges can follow stronger debaters. On closed tasks (MMLU, GSM8KQA, PrOntoQA, TruthfulQA, GPQA) without information asymmetry, Kenton et al. report debate beats consultancy but versus direct QA only GPT-3.5 benefits (p = 0.037), Pro 1.0 shows no difference and Gemma7B and Pro 1.5 do worse; judges are LLMs, not humans.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate helps weaker judges on questions without verifiable evidence, for closed QA tasks with LLM judges and Gemini Pro 1.5 debaters

open_obligations: Note that the quote tool makes the setting close to the fact-checkable case Leike et al. set aside.
Check whether the correct-answer advantage survives without the quote verification tool.
Compare with Kenton et al., who do not find the advantage growing with Elo.
in.other_title: Arguing the correct answer is easier, and the advantage grows with debater persuasiveness
in.rationale: Leike et al. ask whether debate's assumption that truth is easier than lying holds outside easily fact-checkable domains. Khan et al. report debaters get higher Elo when assigned the correct answer and that this advantage grows with aggregate Elo across 20 debaters; however QuALITY debates use a quote tool, so claims are fact-checkable against the text, which is the case Leike et al. exclude.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether telling the truth is easier than lying in debate, for LLM debaters on QuALITY with LLM judges and a quote verification tool

text: Discussing debate (Irving et al., 2018), the authors say more research is needed to determine whether debate is a scalable alignment approach and pose two questions: does debate's central assumption (that telling the truth is easier than lying) hold outside domains of easily fact-checkable statements, and can humans accurately judge the debate even if the debaters have superior persuasion and deception ability?
title: Does debate's honesty assumption hold beyond fact-checkable claims; can humans judge?
